frase_gancho.texto: The Earth squatting, jaws wide open.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the Earth that swallows the Sun, we move on to the Earth that feeds a people. Look at a small stone temple: on its back, an eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus that grows from the body of this very same goddess.

guion_corto.texto: You are standing before Tlaltecuhtli, “Lord or Lady of the Earth,” one of the very few sculptures of this being carved fully in the round. She was almost always carved crushed beneath other stones, so that she would touch the ground; here you see her whole, squatting, in the posture of childbirth, with claws, her face looking up at the sky and her mouth open. She is ready to swallow the dead and the Sun every evening. She wears a necklace of hands and hearts, with a skull hanging from it. Because of this resemblance to [the Coatlicue](mna_s06_coatlicue), when she was found during the construction of the Metro, she was nicknamed “the Coatlicue of the Metro.” She is the Earth as both a hungry monster and a mother.

guion_largo.texto:
In the beginning, the Mexica say, there was water, and on the water floated a monster, Tlaltecuhtli, with mouths at her joints. Quetzalcóatl and Tezcatlipoca, the two gods you already know from the entrance and from Tula, turned into serpents and tore her apart: one half rose and became the sky; the other, the earth. The other gods, to console her, said that everything necessary would come from her body: from her hair, the trees and flowers; from her skin, the grass; from her eyes, the springs and caves; from her mouth, the rivers and mountains.

The myth has a disturbing ending. They say the Earth wept at night, asking for hearts, and that she would bear no fruit unless she was given blood. From this the pact is born: the earth gives maize; the people respond with offerings. It is the same pact you already saw in [the Coatlicue](mna_s06_coatlicue) and that you will see in the [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol). Everything in the Mexica Hall revolves around a single idea: nothing is received without giving something back.

Observe her posture. She is squatting, with her knees raised and her arms bent: the posture of childbirth, which for the Mexica was also the posture of combat, because a woman giving birth was fighting a battle. Her hands and feet end in claws, and at her joints there are eyes and mouths. Her head looks upward, with her mouth open and her tongue out, ready to receive the Sun when it sets.

That is why you almost never see her from the front. Tlaltecuhtli was sculpted on the side that touched the ground, at the base of monoliths such as the Coatlicue and the [head of Coyolxauhqui](mna_s06_coyolxauhqui), so that she would be in contact with the earth she represented. What's more, the famous [Teocalli](mna_s06_teocalli_guerra_sagrada) that comes next has Tlaltecuhtli on its back, and from her body springs the prickly pear cactus. Here, in contrast, she was carved whole, standing on her own feet, and that is why she is so rare.

Her discovery has a very Mexican anecdote. She was found during the construction of Line 1 of the Metro, in the late 1960s, near Pino Suárez station. It was a time when the city was being excavated from below, and archaeology worked at the pace of the machinery. At that same station another famous find appeared, a small circular temple dedicated to the wind god, Ehécatl, which can still be seen today inside the Metro. Two gods of nature, one of wind and one of earth, hidden beneath a modern city.

The nickname, “Coatlicue of the Metro,” is a good example of how we learn. Those who saw her for the first time linked her to the Coatlicue because of the necklace of hands and hearts and the skull. Later it was confirmed that she was not the Coatlicue, but the Earth herself. The two resemble each other because they are two faces of the same idea: the earth that gives and that claims.

She is not the only Tlaltecuhtli to have appeared in the center of the city. In 2006, next to the Templo Mayor, archaeologists found another, gigantic, on a monolith weighing several tons, still bearing traces of red paint. The more the Zócalo is excavated, the more this goddess appears. Perhaps it is because the entire city sits on her body.

And that is the most impressive thing: this figure, which looks like a monster, is in fact the ground we walk on, the root of everything that Mexico eats.

texto: Observe the posture: knees raised, as in childbirth
Look for the necklace of hands and hearts and the skull that hangs from it
Notice the claws and the face looking upward

texto.Material: Andesite carved in the round with traces of red pigment
texto.Origin: Historic Center, Mexico City (found in September 1967 during Metro construction at Pino Suárez / Izazaga)
texto.Dimensions: 120 cm high x 85 cm wide x 80 cm thick

texto.pregunta: Myth: This sculpture is Coatlicue, the mother of Huitzilopochtli.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is Tlaltecuhtli, the Earth as a devouring monster. It was called “Coatlicue of the Metro” because of the resemblance of the necklace, but she is not the same goddess.
